newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Commerce's Daley vows aggressive Africa policy.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Commerce's Daley vows aggressive Africa policy.

text.p: U.S. Commerce Secretary William Daley said on Monday his department will make an aggressive effort to promote U.S. trade and investment with Africa.

Daley said at a conference on business opportunities in South Africa that as part of that push, he will lead a delegation of U.S. business leaders on a trade mission to Africa in early 1998 and will make sure his agency's export assistance centres promote opportunities in Africa.

South African Trade and Industry Minister Alec Erwin told the group of more than 200 U.S. and South African business leaders that the country's economic reconstruction was moving beyond the process of stabilisation and into a phase where new projects were coming on stream.

The U.S. Trade and Development Agency, one of the sponsors of the two-day conference, released a list of some 45 new South African projects in transportation, environment, telecommunications, industry, power and tourism that could offer business opportunities for U.S. companies.

The focus on South Africa is part of a Clinton administration initiative on Africa that focuses on trade and investment, rather than direct government aid, as a way to boost economic development. Daley said South Africa could be a good place to start for many U.S. businesses.

"We are seeking to emphasise the significant opportunity, not only in South Africa but in the entire continent," Daley said. "Part of our message today is that South Africa clearly is an economy and a market well worthy of very serious market attention.
"The other side of that message is that South Africa itself is both a platform and also a launching point for exploring the other African markets that U.S. firms may have overlooked," he added.
Erwin told conference participants that South Africa sees the region as forming a bridge of trade and investment with Latin America and Asia.

"If the Southern African economy revives, if Africa revives, then a bridge forms between the rapidly growing areas of East Asia, particularly those in the Indian Ocean rim and Latin America and a new configuration of economic interaction begins to become a reality in the world," Erwin said.
